'''''Oxalis pes-caprae''''' is a species of [[heterostyly|tristylous]] yellow-flowering plant in the wood sorrel family [[Oxalidaceae]]. '''''Oxalis cernua''''' is a less common synonym for this species. It is commonly known as '''African wood-sorrel''', '''Bermuda buttercup,''' '''Bermuda sorrel''', '''buttercup oxalis''', '''Cape sorrel''', '''English weed''', '''goat's-foot''', '''sourgrass''', '''soursob''', or '''soursop'''; '''{{Langx|af|suring}}'''; '''{{Langx|ar|hommayda}}''' (حميضة). 

Some of the most common names for the plant reference its sour taste owing to [[oxalic acid]] present in its tissues. Indigenous to South Africa, the plant has become a [[pest plant]] in different parts of the world that is difficult to eradicate because of how it propagates through underground [[bulb]]s.

== Name ==
''Oxalis pes-caprae'' is often called by the common name ''[[sourgrass|sourgrass]]'' due to its moderately [[Sour|sour flavor]]. This sourness is caused by an exceptionally high content of [[oxalic acid]].

The specific epithet ''pes-caprae'' means 'goat's-foot', possibly in reference to the shape of the leaf.

==Description==

The ''Oxalis pes-caprae'' flower is [[floral symmetry|actinomorphic]], with a [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] composed of five free or slightly fused [[sepal]]s, a [[sympetaly|sympetalous]] [[corolla (flower)|corolla]] composed of five fused petals, an [[androecium]] composed of ten free [[stamen]]s in two ranks, and a compound [[gynoecium|pistil]]. Native populations in South Africa are [[Heterostyly|heterostylous]], flowers of long-styled plants have a [[stigma (botany)|stigma]] held above the two ranks of stamens, mid-styled plants have the stigma in between the two ranks of stamens and short-styled plants have a stigma below both ranks of stamen. In the non-native range the plants largely reproduce vegetatively and many populations have only one style length and the plants never produce seed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rottenberg |first1=Aaron |last2=Parker |first2=John S. |title=Asexual populations of the invasive weed are genetically variable |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B: Biological Sciences |date=7 May 2004 |volume=271 |issue=suppl_4 |pages=S206-8 |doi=10.1098/rsbl.2003.0135|pmid=15252985 |pmc=1810042 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Castro|first1=Sílvia|last2=Ferrero|first2=Victoria|last3=Costa|first3=Joana|last4=Sousa|first4=Ana João|last5=Castro|first5=Mariana|last6=Navarro|first6=Luis|last7=Loureiro|first7=João|date=2013-08-01|title=Reproductive strategy of the invasive Oxalis pes-caprae: distribution patterns of floral morphs, ploidy levels and sexual reproduction|journal=Biological Invasions|language=en|volume=15|issue=8|pages=1863–1875|doi=10.1007/s10530-013-0414-2|bibcode=2013BiInv..15.1863C |s2cid=17974421|issn=1573-1464}}</ref>

Like most African ''Oxalis'' species, it produces adventitious subterranean [[propagule]]s. These take the form of true [[bulb]]s in botanical terms, which is unusual among [[dicotyledon]]s. ''O. pes-caprae'' produces small bulbs copiously, whereas most other African species produce fewer, larger bulbs.

==As an invasive species==
[[File:Oxalis pes-caprae seedling from bulb.jpg|thumb|Invasive ''O. pes-caprae'' forms peanut-sized bulbs that survive the dry California summer, then sprout after rainfall.|right]]

Indigenous to South Africa, ''Oxalis pes-caprae'' is an [[invasive species]] and [[noxious weed]] in many other parts of the world, including the United States (particularly coastal California),<ref>[http://www.cal-ipc.org/ip/management/plant_profiles/Oxalis_pes-caprae.php  Cal-IPC profile]</ref> Europe,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Papini|first1=A.|last2=Signorini|first2=M.A.|last3=Foggi|first3=B.|last4=Della Giovampaola|first4=E.|last5=Ongaro|first5=L.|last6=Vivona|first6=L.|last7=Santosuosso|first7=U.|last8=Tani|first8=C.|last9=Bruschi|first9=P.|date=2017-12-29|title=History vs. legend: retracing invasion and spread of Oxalis pes-caprae L. in Europe and the Mediterranean area|journal=PLOS ONE|language=en|volume=12|issue=12|article-number=e0190237|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0190237|pmid=29287103 |pmc=5747460 |bibcode=2017PLoSO..1290237P |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[The Middle East]], and Australia.<ref>{{cite web |title=Soursob (Oxalis pes-caprae) (Nox) |url=http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/weeds_herbs_perennial_soursob |work=Victorian Resources Online |author=Department of Primary Industries, Victoria, Australia |access-date=8 June 2017}}</ref>

===Control===
The plant has a reputation for being very difficult to eliminate by mechanical methods once it has spread over an area of land.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Elmore, C. L.  |author2=Cudney, D. W.  |name-list-style=amp |editor=Ohlendorf, B. |date= January 2002|title=Creeping Woodsorrel and Bermuda Buttercup |journal=Pest Notes |volume=Publication 7444 |page=2 |publisher=Agricultural & Natural Resources, University of California |url=http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7444.html |access-date=25 June 2010}}</ref> The weed propagates largely through its underground bulbs and this is one reason why it is so difficult to eradicate, as pulling up the plant, even with the roots, can leave some of the bulbs behind. Soil in which the plant has grown is generally contaminated with many small bulbs.{{cn|date=June 2026}} 

Kluge & Claassens (1990) reported a potential biocontrol agent using ''[[Klugeana]] philoxalis'', a larval feeder on shoots of ''O. pes-caprae''.<ref>Kluge, R. L.; Claassens, M.; "''Klugeana philoxalis'' Geertsema (Noctuidae: Cuculliinae), the first potential biological control agent for the weed Oxalis pes-caprae L."; ''Journal of the Entomological Society of Southern Africa'' 1990 Vol. 53 No. 2 pp. 191–198</ref><ref>{{cite web | access-date=2009-12-22 | title=''Oxalis pes-caprae'' | url=http://www.dpi.vic.gov.au/DPI/Vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/weeds_herbs_perennial_soursob }}</ref>

Two studies have reported successful control using two different non-selective, consumer-grade [[herbicides]]. [[Imazapyr]]<ref>{{cite web | access-date=2022-04-01 | title=''Weed Control Methods Handbook: Tools and Techniques for Use in Natural Areas'' 7h.1, 2001 | url=http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/ | archive-date=2007-05-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070527143137/http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/ }}</ref> applied in late March 2016 at low concentration appeared to completely prevent re-sprouting of ''O. pes-caprae'' bulbs in the [[San Francisco]] area.<ref>{{cite web | access-date=2022-04-01 | title=''Management of Bermuda Buttercup (Oxalis pes caprae ) in the Peninsula Watershed of the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission'' 2017 | url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/2017_Symposium-Managing-Bermuda-buttercup-in-SF-Pub-Util-Thomas.pdf}}</ref> [[Glyphosate]]<ref>{{cite web | access-date=2022-04-01 | title=''Weed Control Methods Handbook: Tools and Techniques for Use in Natural Areas'' 7e.1, 2001 | url=http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/ | archive-date=2007-05-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070527143137/http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/ }}</ref> was used successfully on a Mediterranean island, reported in 2019.<ref>{{cite journal | access-date=2022-04-01 | title=''Treatment by glyphosate-based herbicide allowed recovering native species after Oxalis pes-caprae L. invasion: indications from a Mediterranean island'' 2019 | journal=Plant Biosystems | date=3 September 2019 | volume=153 | issue=5 | pages=651–659 | doi=10.1080/11263504.2018.1536083 | s2cid=91677579 | url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/11263504.2018.1536083| last1=Lazzaro | first1=Lorenzo | last2=Ferretti | first2=Giulio | last3=Bianchi | first3=Elisabetta | last4=Benesperi | first4=Renato | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Hazards==
{{Original research|section|date=November 2012}}
The leaves or roots are used in some parts of the world as a food,<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bown|first=Deni|title=Encyclopedia of herbs & their uses|date=1995|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|others=Herb Society of America|isbn=0-7894-0184-3|oclc=32166152}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Sturtevant|first=E. Lewis|title=Sturtevant's edible plants of the world|date=1972|publisher=Dover Publications|others=U. P. Hedrick|isbn=0-486-20459-6|location=New York|oclc=718374}}</ref> although the high levels of calcium oxalate in the plant may bear some risks. Such risks can be reduced if the plant parts are boiled first.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chai|first1=Weiwen|last2=Liebman|first2=Michael|date=April 2005|title=Effect of Different Cooking Methods on Vegetable Oxalate Content|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jf048128d|journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry|language=en|volume=53|issue=8|pages=3027–3030|doi=10.1021/jf048128d|pmid=15826055|bibcode=2005JAFC...53.3027C |issn=0021-8561|url-access=subscription}}</ref> [[Oxalic acid]] is toxic in large quantities, a concern in regions such as southern Australia where ''Oxalis pes-caprae'' grows invasively in enormous quantities and in high densities.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} Various sources suggest that ''oxalis'' ingestion causes calcium oxalate kidney stones, but clinical experience and physiological considerations make it unlikely that any realistic intake of ''Oxalis'' would affect human liability to [[kidney stone]]s.{{citation needed|date=November 2020}} Accordingly, some Australian references to the hazards of ''oxalis'' to livestock tend to be dismissive of this risk.{{citation needed|date=November 2020}}

However, in spite of its comparatively benign nature, where it has become dominant in pastures, as sometimes happens outside South Africa, ''Oxalis pes-caprae'' certainly can cause dramatic stock losses. For example, when hungry stock, such as sheep released just after being shorn, are let out to graze in a lush growth of ''Oxalis pes-caprae'', they may gorge on the plant, with fatal results, as has been found in South Australia at least.<ref>Bull, L.; ''Australian Veterinary Journal'', 1929, Vol. 5 p. 60</ref>

Such stock fatalities patently have little logical connection with the presence or absence of oxalate kidney stones. For one thing, the fatal effects on sheep are far too rapid to result from the growth of bulk kidney stones. The plant has been found to be nutritious, but too acidic to be good fodder, largely being left untouched by grazing stock. When stock do consume large quantities, the effects typically involve death in several weeks with symptoms suggesting chronic oxalate poisoning, including [[tetany]], or sudden death with extensive renal damage.<ref name="watt">Watt, John Mitchell; Breyer-Brandwijk, Maria Gerdina: ''The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa'' 2nd ed Pub. E & S Livingstone 1962</ref> Such damage suggests the twofold effect of calcium immobilisation (the tetany) and the formation of Calcium Oxalate Monohydrate [[raphide]]s in the kidney tissue.<ref name="pmid19852621">{{cite journal |author=McMartin K |title=Are calcium oxalate crystals involved in the mechanism of acute renal failure in ethylene glycol poisoning? |journal=Clin Toxicol |volume=47 |issue=9 |pages=859–69 |date=November 2009 |pmid=19852621 |doi=10.3109/15563650903344793 |s2cid=26702305 }}</ref> The histotoxic effects of the raphides in kidney have by now been investigated.<ref>Wiessner, John H.; Hasegawa, Andrew T.;  Hung, Linda Y.;  Mandel, Gretchen S.;  Mandel, Neil S.; "-- Mechanisms of calcium oxalate crystal attachment to injured renal collecting duct cells"; ''Kidney International'' (2001) 59, 637–644; {{doi|10.1046/j.1523-1755.2001.059002637.x}}</ref>

Oxalis poisoning of stock is not a serious [[forage]] concern in South African pastures, unless exceptionally favoured by [[overgrazing]].

== Uses ==
The plant is palatable and in modest quantities is reasonably harmless to humans and livestock. In South Africa it is a traditional ingredient in dishes such as [[waterblommetjiebredie]] ('water flower stew').<ref name="isbn0-7981-4919-1">{{cite book |author=S. J. A. de Villiers |title=Cook and Enjoy |publisher=NB Publishers |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-7981-4919-8}}</ref>

The plant has been used in various ways as a source of oxalic acid, as food, and in folk medicine. The raw bulbs have been used to deal with [[tapeworm]] and possibly other worms. The plant has been used as a diuretic, possibly hazardously. The lateral underground runners, which tend to be fleshy, have been eaten raw or boiled and served with milk.<ref name="watt" /> The golden petals can be used to produce a yellow [[dye]].<ref>{{cite news |author=Michael Tortorello |date=April 5, 2012 |title=A New Generation Discovers Grow-It-Yourself Dyes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/05/garden/a-new-generation-discovers-grow-it-yourself-dyes.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref>
